title: Product discovery is changing: how to design experiences for people who research with AI
description: Part of discovery happens outside your site, in search and AI assistants. Clear, consistent information helps people and systems decide.

related.title: WhatsApp Next
related.body: In practice: blog, landing page and campaign telling the same story at every touchpoint.

blocks.text: For a long time, digital discovery followed a familiar path: people searched, opened results, compared pages and reached a decision.

That path still exists, but now it lives alongside new forms of search and assistance. People can ask an AI to compare alternatives, summarize features or help them figure out which solution fits their needs.
For those of us working in UX and content, this raises an important question: how do you help someone make a good decision when part of the discovery happens outside the product's interface?
The journey doesn't necessarily start on your site

Someone might land on a product page after reading an AI-generated comparison, getting a recommendation or checking a summary. They may arrive with a hypothesis about the product, but they may also bring an incomplete or incorrect expectation.
That makes consistency across channels even more important. The page needs to quickly confirm what the product does, who it's for, what its limitations are and what sets the offer apart.
This isn't about writing to please an algorithm. It's about making information clear, consistent and verifiable for the people and systems trying to interpret it.
Organize content to answer real questions
Instead of producing pages full of adjectives, identify the questions that help your audience decide. For a SaaS, for example:

items: What problem does it solve, and for whom?
How does it work day to day?
Which tools does it integrate with?
How much does it cost and what's included?

blocks.text: The answers should be specific and consistent with the product. When a piece of information isn't available, don't make it up. Explain what is known and point to the right source.
Don't hide limitations behind a marketing promise
When an AI summarizes a page, nuance can disappear. Essential information shouldn't be scattered across vague copy or tucked into hard-to-find elements.

Use descriptive headings, comparison tables when they make sense, requirement lists, usage examples and clear explanations of limitations. On pricing pages, spell out what each plan includes. On feature pages, separate what's already available from what's planned.
This also helps people who don't use AI. Good information architecture improves understanding in any channel.
Design comparisons that support decisions
A useful comparison table doesn't need to list dozens of features. It should highlight the criteria that matter for the choice.

items: Identify the criteria that really set the options apart.
Explain technical terms in plain language.
Show limits and conditions, not just advantages.
Let people compare without losing the page's context.
Don't visually highlight an option that doesn't meet the need.
Test whether people can justify their choice based on the information available.

blocks.text: The goal is to reduce the effort of comparing, not to push everyone toward the most expensive plan.
Measure discovery quality, not just traffic

Combine quantitative and qualitative indicators: internal searches with no results, paths to conversion, clicks on comparisons and documentation, recurring questions to support or sales, doubts observed in testing and lead quality by channel, when attribution is reliable.

Don't automatically attribute a conversion to an AI tool just because the person says they used one. Attribution can be incomplete. Use source surveys, analytics data and feedback, and be clear about the limitations.
Clear content is part of the product experience
The marketing page, the documentation, the help center and the interface need to tell the same story. If each channel describes a feature differently, people will struggle to understand what's real.

Build a simple matrix: user question, available answer, source responsible for the information and where the answer shows up. That helps you find gaps and contradictions before trying to fix everything with more content.
AI-mediated discovery doesn't remove the need for UX. It makes clear, consistent and decision-ready information even more important.
